articles.description: The Lycurgus Cup, a world-renowned 4th-century A.D. artifact housed in the British Museum, is constructed of "dichroic" glass that shifts from jade green in reflected light to ruby red in transmitted light. articles.title: Want to be happier? Oxford research says ask yourself these 3 questions
articles.description: What does it take to be happy? Three simple and surprising questions may hold the answer, research found. While most of us seek more money and greater achievement as paths to happiness, these questions are all about connection. They’re more strongly associated with self-measured life satisfaction than either money or success. That’s according to the 2025 World Happiness Report published by Oxford University and based on a study of people in 147 countries. The questions are: How often do you eat meals with other people, rather than alone? Do you generally expect strangers to be kind and trustworthy? How often do you do things for other people, such as making donations, volunteering, or helping strangers? This may all sound like wishful thinking, but the research shows that, while economic security and career satisfaction contribute to happiness, these prosocial factors make a much bigger difference. If you want to be happy, 1. Eat with others This is a rare instance where the report’s happiness advice coincides with frequently offered success advice to never have lunch alone. Lunching at your desk can mean missing out on valuable opportunities for networking or relationship building. It turns out it can also mean missing the chance to be happier by building a stronger social connection. Research suggests that we often expect spending time alone will make us happier than being with others, especially people we don’t know well. But then when we do spend time with others, it makes us happier than we expected. The research looked at whether subjects ate with others or alone for lunch and dinner (it didn’t consider breakfast). Happiness appeared to peak at a whopping 13 lunches or dinners with others per week, which is more meal sharing than most Americans do. But it showed that any amount of eating with others will increase your happiness. So go ahead and grab yourself a lunch or dinner date, even if the person you invite isn’t a valuable business connection. It will make you feel more connected, and boost your happiness, too. 2. Expect strangers to be trustworthy If you dropped your wallet on the street, how likely is it that someone would return it to you with the money still inside? World Happiness Report researchers found that most people underestimate how often they would get their wallets back in this scenario. They also found that those who thought the wallet return was likelier also tended to be happier. But while eating with others would be an excellent business practice, trusting strangers probably isn’t. In a world where not every stranger is trustworthy, how do you balance the benefits of trusting strangers against the very real risks of trusting the wrong one? But consider how many breakout companies are built on the outlandish idea that you can indeed trust strangers. Amazon, Facebook, Etsy, eBay, and other online marketplaces let strangers buy and sell from each other. Uber, Rover, and other such companies encourage us to put our safety, or that of our beloved pets, into the hands of people we’ve never met. Why do we trust these strangers? Because other strangers left reviews saying we could. It seems illogical and yet it works. Does this mean you should blindly accept business propositions from people you don’t know without any due diligence? Of course not. You also should not leave your wallet in the street and assume someone will bring it back to you. But if you tend to automatically distrust anyone you don’t know, try to change that mindset. It will make you happier. It might make the people you do business with happier too. 3. Be kind to others The report looked at three types of benevolent acts: donating, volunteering, and helping strangers. “The well-being benefits of benevolent acts depend on why and how people engage in them. Both helpers and recipients experience greater happiness from caring and sharing when they do so in the context of caring connections, choice, and clear positive impact,” the researchers write. For one thing, choice is important. If you hear about a disaster in your area and feel inspired to make a donation to help, that’s likelier to make you happy than, say, feeling compelled to donate to a charity because your biggest customer or your boss has asked you to. And both giver and receiver of a benevolent act benefit more when they can see a clear positive impact. If you make a donation or volunteer your time to help rebuild a local park, and then spend time there watching people enjoy the park, you’ll get a bigger happiness boost. If the people there know you helped out and can thank you, they will too. Performing benevolent acts gets you the biggest happiness result for the smallest effort. Being kind to other people doesn’t just make you happy, it makes them happy too, World Happiness Report researchers found. That may inspire those people to their own acts of kindness, inspiring others to be kind, and so on. Pretty soon, you might have a self-perpetuating happiness machine. That could benefit any organization or community. —Minda Zetlin This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com. Inc. is the voice of the American entrepreneur. We inspire, inform, and document the most fascinating people in business: the risk-takers, the innovators, and the ultra-driven go-getters that represent the most dynamic force in the American economy.

articles.title: How a samurai classic shared Japanese values with the West
articles.description: In 1899, Inazo Nitobe published a book in English called "Bushido: The Soul of Japan." Nitobe was born into a samurai family and later became a Christian. He wrote the book after a Belgian legal scholar asked him how Japan taught morality without religious instruction in its schools. Nitobe came to realize the answer was the samurai ethics he had grown up with. He described them through seven virtues: rectitude, courage, benevolence, politeness, veracity, honor and loyalty.

articles.title: Moving past outdated models: a seminar exploring religion and public health
articles.description: Editors of the Handbook on Religion and Health: Pathways for a Turbulent Future Gary Gunderson and Teresa Cutts ("TC"), visited the Bloomberg School of Public Health on Thursday, Oct. 22 to give their talk "Watersheds: Moving beyond Downstream/Upstream Metaphors to Advance Public Health." Gunderson, Professor of Faith and Health of the Public at Wake Forest University, and Cutts, health psychologist, shared their perspectives on faith-health in the fourth iteration of the Public Health and Religion Seminar Series sponsored by the Office of the Provost. With Dean of the Bloomberg School of Public Health Keshia Pollack Porter in the room, the organizers highlighted the series goal of encouraging discussion of topics not typically brought up on campus. Gunderson and TC are leaders of the growing FaithHealth Movement, which aims to establish partnerships between spiritual communities and health-care professionals with the ultimate goal of improving health. They do this by mobilizing religious communities to emotionally and spiritually support hospital patients, help with meals, provide transportation to and from doctor's appointments, and more. Gunderson opened with a guiding question. "What do we do with our life?" He emphasized that forums bringing together many spiritual and professional perspectives can be valuable places to discuss this topic. "The movement itself is still quite young, and it's because it's especially appropriate to these times of what I will call radical discontinuity: when government, policy, culture, religion, every way of understanding the world right now is in a time of fundamental discontinuity... That's exactly when we need new minds on the job, new thoughts, new language to help us not repair but navigate to the future," he said. He went on to introduce the focus of the talk - challenging traditional public health language to better suit spiritual spaces. In particular, he discussed about discarding the upstream-downstream framework and replacing it with the watershed metaphor. The upstream-downstream framework is often described and can be understood using the following story. At a point on the local river, health-care workers notice people floating downstream, struggling to get out. The workers rush to help the people but also struggle with the volume of affected individuals, the lack of available resources, and understaffing (downstream). Public health workers decide to walk up the river and understand why people are falling into the river in the first place; could it be a broken bridge, a lack of safety rails, or something else (upstream)? This story highlights the two strategies that can be used when addressing public health issues: the downstream, reactive intervention strategy, or the upstream, proactive prevention strategy. The framework addresses issues by assuming there is one root cause of an issue and that everyone experiencing the upstream trauma will have the same outcome. It oversimplifies issues that are anything but simple. This is contrasted with the watershed framework. Watersheds are inherently complex. Tributaries converge and diverge at seemingly random places and the whole system intricately interacts with things like rain, cattle grazing, settling patterns and more. Gunderson used a LiDAR image - a 3D representation of a surface captured by laser - of the Mississippi River Watershed to make the point that public health issues, like watersheds, are much more complex than the original framework lets on. "That's really the heart of the LiDAR image. It doesn't just show you where the river is. The LiDAR shows you where the river has been," he said. As a result, it also shows us where it may be going. He continued on by critiquing another traditional public health metric often used to determine where public health funding is best spent: the "leading causes of death." "The leading cause of death, which drives almost all public health budgeting, [is a] bad idea. It's about half of an idea. The other half of the idea is life, and so one of the critical ideas that we'll talk about a little bit is leading causes of life... [We will consider] the interplay between moving from the simplicity of upstream-downstream to invite the radical complexity of watersheds, and then move towards leading causes of life to balance leading causes of death." These leading causes of life, which were his focus for much of the talk, included connection, hope, agency and considering the vocabulary of the psychosocial and spiritual determinants of health. TC then stepped up to share a story from Johann Hari's book Lost Connections, in which a community rallies behind a man suffering from depression and helps him out of the hardship. "[The story] illustrates how neighbors, community can come around and just listen and look at what are some real-life situations and things [where] we can get to the root of the problems," she said. She went on to comment on modern psychopharmacological prescription practices and emphasized that communities, including spiritual communities, can be powerful resources in supporting and educating those experiencing mental illness. Gunderson closed with a call for intergenerational and interdisciplinary collaboration on a path to make a better future. Acknowledging the complexity of the issues facing society, he expressed optimism for the FaithHealth Movement's ability to address them head on. The next Public Health and Religion Seminar will take place Wednesday, Nov. 18 at noon at the School of Public Health where John Blevins will give his talk "Religion and Public Health After the Liberal Protestant Consensus: Past Partnerships, Present Tensions, and New Terms of Engagement."

articles.title: Broncos buck the haters again
articles.description: Three years ago I published an article titled: "The Resurgence of the Denver Broncos" in what was an optimistic, albeit slightly delusional (sue me for being a Broncos fan), look at the improvement of the Broncos in the aftermath of the infamous Miami massacre. After trading significant draft capital for a head coach, the 2023 season could not have started off worse for the Mile High faithful. Questions surrounded the quarterback, the aging players on the roster and, most importantly, the coaching staff. When local beat writers start publishing articles titled: "Broncos need to fire defensive coordinator Vance Joseph," there usually isn't a clear path back to success. Nevertheless, the Broncos stayed the course, and as I remarked on in the article, breakouts from young players like Ja'Quan McMillian have helped to build what has been one of the two or three best defenses in the world ever since. That is not to say there hasn't been significant change since 2023 though… in fact it is quite the contrary. One of the defining characteristics of Sean Payton's tenure with the Broncos has been the influx of "his guys". While his infatuation with keeping guys like Lil'Jordan Humphrey and Alex Singleton on the team may frustrate the fanbase, the additions of Malcolm Roach, Zach Allen and Wil Lutz have made the team significantly stronger. This is all without mentioning the cog that helps everything turn: the ever-controversial, much-maligned quarterback that is Bo Nix. Say what you will about Bo, but his win-loss record is amongst the best since entering the league, and he has an undeniable clutch factor that helped the Broncos take down the Bills in a playoff shootout. He has certainly had some struggles and is currently experiencing what can only be described as a bad case of the "yips", but he and Sean Payton know how to win games together. However, all of this could not be accomplished without former Broncos Head Coach, Vance Joseph. After a short (and disappointing) stint in the driver's seat, Joseph moved to Arizona to take over as defensive coordinator for the Cardinals. Four years passed in Glendale before GM George Paton rang his phone and brought him back into the building as the team's defensive coordinator. In the three years since his hiring, the Broncos have conceded the third least points in the league whilst recording twenty-nine more sacks than the next best team during that same timespan. This is a testament to Joseph's blitz-heavy scheme that has perfected the nuances of disguised pressure. McMillian has proved to be one of the most effective DBs at causing pressure from the nickel, and combined with the lightning speed of Nik Bonitto and steady production from Allen, the Broncos defense is a force to be reckoned with. As we shift our attention to the 2026 season, Denver has faced arguably the most difficult opening schedule in the league with the Chiefs, Jags, Niners, Rams, Seahawks, Cardinals and Chargers. In spite of this, they have a 5 - 2 record and are heading into a much easier part of their schedule. Whilst the offense has looked far from perfect, the defense has continued their strong performances from years prior and ultimately will be their calling card when the going gets tough. The recipe for playoff success in Denver is the offense returning to a league-average, or slightly above, level. We saw how close the Broncos got to the Super Bowl in 2025, even with a backup quarterback playing in a blizzard-affected game against the Patriots, and so they will try to recreate that formula in 2026. The injection of speed with the addition of Jaylen Waddle was meant to take them over the top in this chase for a repeat AFC title, but so far the results have been middling. The key with Waddle will be trying to get him the ball in space and on deep shots: Currently the Broncos have the lowest ADOT in the league (5.1 yards per play). While a low ADOT is not an issue inherently, the fact that a lot of these targets have been directed towards their less formidable playmakers is where the concerns start to seep in. While leading the team in targets, Waddle's overall share is not where it should be. Denver's running backs have occupied a significant portion of the offensive gameplan (45 targets to Waddle's 38), often leaving the Broncos behind the sticks and in long and predictable third down scenarios. When an opposing defense is aware that you need to throw the ball eight to ten yards on third down, they are able to pin their ears back and get after the quarterback, ironically something that Denver's own defense is so effective at. Waddle's role should thrive in a Sean Payton offense that has the ability to air it out downfield, but because the team is more often than not caught in long passing downs, his effectiveness is severely neutralised. With Jonah Coleman coming off of the IR, the Broncos should be able to establish a more consistent run-game, helping them get into more manageable down-to-down situations. From this, utilising the play-action game and occasional roll-outs will help maximalize the Broncos offense and their primary playmakers skills. Against the Cardinals, Bo showcased his ability to make plays with his legs (see his 62-yard rushing touchdown). Holding the opposition accountable on the ground will help to create more wide-open lanes for Nix to get the ball to Waddle and help this offense return to their late-season selves from 2025/26. I have faith that we will see Denver separate from the pack with some positive regression from the offense. People may get their jokes off about Bo Nix as a quarterback, but there are now years of proof that he can help this team reach the highest level and operate a functioning offense. The Broncos are not a team to be taken lightly, and Sean Payton and his guys will continue to put out a product of football that will make the Denver faithful happy to turn on their TV every Sunday.

articles.title: A New Space for STEM in East Baltimore
articles.description: For students at Collington Square Elementary and Middle School in East Baltimore, the beginning of the 2026-2026 school year brought a new opportunity to explore science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM). The school recently opened the Cal Ripken, Sr. STEM Center, named after the Baltimore Orioles player, scout, coach and manager. The center, revealed back in August, is designed to give students hands-on experiences while developing skills in critical thinking, problem-solving and collaboration. Hopkins, continuing its work of giving back to the East Baltimore community, provided financial and logistical support for the project. The center is part of the Cal Ripken, Sr. Foundation's larger STEM initiative spanning across the country, providing students with opportunities for early exposure to STEM and hands-on learning. With more than 890 STEM centers, the foundation claims it has reached more than 377,000 children. That access could make STEM subjects feel less abstract and more tangible for underrepresented communities. Rather than encountering science and mathematics solely through textbooks and lectures, students can use a dedicated space to experiment, solve problems, collaborate and explore their own questions in a way that keeps interest and attention. The new center also builds on a relationship that has been developing between Collington Square and Hopkins. Over the past year, the Johns Hopkins Police Department (JHPD) has partnered with the school through its Police Athletic/Activities League, or PAL. The program has provided mentorship and educational activities for the school's roughly 200 students in pre-K through eighth grade. JHPD officers have participated in activities including chess and financial literacy programs, a holiday toy drive and community events. In an email to The News-Letter, Morgan Jones-Massey, director of the JHPD PAL program, shared the rationale behind this partnership. "The Cal Ripken, Sr. STEM Center aligns with the Johns Hopkins Police Department Police Activities League (PAL) initiatives by supporting educational enrichment, youth engagement, community partnerships, and career exploration," said Jones-Massey wrote. STEM became one of the areas of focus for the partnership. In July, before the center opened, JHPD's PAL program announced plans to bring a STEM program to Collington Square, with as much as $40,000 in technology, resources, and programming at no cost to the school. At the time, Collington Square's community schools coordinator Mikala Nuccio described the program as an important addition because the school did not previously have a STEM resource of this scale. "Exposure is important because it allows students to discover new interests, recognize their potential, and understand opportunities that may not otherwise be available to them." detailed Jones-Massey. She explained the center can help students broaden their perspectives, build confidence, and envision possibilities beyond their immediate environment. That message is particularly significant in STEM, where early exposure can help students begin to see these fields as possibilities for their own futures. A student who experiments with a new technology today may eventually pursue engineering, medicine, computer science, research or another STEM-related career. For Hopkins, the project also reflects a broader commitment to its surrounding community. The University's relationship with Collington Square extends beyond the STEM center, with the PAL program providing opportunities for mentorship, recreation, education and community engagement. Looking beyond the STEM center itself, Jones-Massey explained PAL is focused on addressing the needs of the "whole child," including through educational enrichment, financial literacy and social-emotional programming. "What I want readers to understand is that PAL is about more than police officers interacting with youth; it is about building trust, creating access to opportunities, and investing in the potential of our young people. Our goal is to establish a strong, sustainable foundation at Collington Square that can make a meaningful difference in students' lives while creating a model for potential growth in the future," Jones-Massey wrote.

articles.title: Hopkins Sports in Review (Oct. 19-25): Football return to form with win over Muhlenberg
articles.description: The season continues for all the Hopkins teams as we approach conference championships. Many teams are wrapping up their final games of the regular season before post-season action ensues, and so it's vital to keep up with all the impressive performances on display! If you can, try and get to some games to support the Blue Jays, but in the meantime, let's have a look at the weekly roundup! Football: W (40-14) The Football team has been through an uncharacteristic slump this season, which saw them fall to a 1-5 record prior to their matchup against the Gettysburg Bullets. After a difficult stretch of consecutive road games through Pennsylvania, the Blue Jays hoped to get right back in Baltimore... and get right they did. The first quarter remained low-scoring, with the only points coming from a 22-yard field goal at the end of the period, putting Hopkins up 3-0. Gettysburg would answer back with a touchdown on the next drive, but from then out it was all Hopkins. Three straight touchdowns from the Blue Jays would ensue, two of which were from junior quarterback Luke Baker to senior wide receiver Robby Enright before a 13-yard run gave Hopkins a 17-point lead. The Bullets managed to score a touchdown of their own to begin the final quarter, but Hopkins would swiftly crush their hopes of a comeback with a safety and two rushing touchdowns from their quarterbacks Baker and sophomore Milan Desai. The team will be taking on Muhlenberg on Oct. 31 at Homewood Field, so be sure to get down and support them as conference play continues! Field Hockey: W (6-0), W (3-1) Women's Field Hockey have been one of the most impressive teams all season, and this past week was no different! Coming up against the Washington College Shorewomen in Chestertown, the pressure was on to continue their win-streak that stretches back to the start of the month. This was no problem for the Blue Jays, as they made light work of their conference opponents... Junior midfielder Kaitlin Coward scored the first three goals of the game to complete her first career hattrick! With such a dominant opening from Hopkins there was not much room for Washington College to get back in the game. Only managing one shot in the contest, it's safe to say that they were comprehensively outplayed by Hopkins. The ninth-ranked Hopkins side then welcomed Haverford into their home field for a day that honored the seniors on the team. With a victory they would be able to solidify a bye into the Centennial Conference semifinals, so the stakes were high. Once again though, they were up to the task. Senior midfielder Eliza Vander scored within the first two minutes, before sophomore Sarah Chilton made it two in the second period. Haverford would score and bring the margin to a single goal, but an insurance goal from Kaitlin Coward in the fourth would cement the crucial victory for Hopkins! Women's Soccer: W (3-0) Coming into the weekend, the Women's Soccer team were ranked 18th in the nation! They also were defending a six-game win-streak against their opponents, Muhlenberg, so all the cards were on the table. Up to the task, Hopkins scored two first half goals to take a commanding lead over their conference rivals. Freshman forward Katie Derby would register the first score of the match in the 17th minute of action, her fifth of the year, before junior midfielder Carolyn Johnson would also register her fifth of the year in the 26th minute! The Hopkins defense was barely tested as they conceded only two shots for the entire contest, both of which were not on target. Junior midfielder Kendall Frederick was the final scorer of the afternoon as her 76th minute goal put the Blue Jays up 3-0 in a virtually unassailable position!

articles.title: Science news in review: Oct. 26
articles.description: Let's dive into the latest in scientific news and explore recent breakthroughs, discoveries and advancements that are shaping our understanding of the world. This week's column explores drought responses, antimatter particles and artificial planetary molecules. Root cells and drought response Researchers studying Arabidopsis thaliana roots recently discovered that plant cells have an additional layer of identity. Scientists traditionally classify root cells according to their cell type and developmental stage, but by analyzing activity in tens of thousands of individual cells, they found that cells across many different root tissues can exist in one of the two transcriptional states. One of these states activates hundreds of genes associated with environmental responses. In the environment-regulated state (ERS), two cells belonging to the same traditional cell type can behave differently depending on whether this program is switched on or off. The researchers also found that the proportion of cells entering this state changed depending on the plant's environment. Under water-deficit conditions, more root cells switched into the ERS-positive state. This response was also connected to abscisic acid (ABA), a plant hormone that plays a significant role in responding to droughts. Plants unable to properly produce or detect ABA had substantially fewer cells entering this state. This finding suggests that plants may adapt by changing the proportion of cells operating in an environmentally responsive mode. By understanding this process, researchers are better equipped with context to engineer crops with improved drought tolerance and inform plant growth in environments such as vertical farms. Controlling an antimatter particle Physicists at Northwestern University have successfully isolated and controlled a single positron in the quantum state. Positrons normally annihilate when they contact ordinary matter. The researchers suspended a positron inside a Penning trap using carefully controlled electric and magnetic fields within a vacuum. After cooling the system to about 0.3K above absolute zero, the positron reached its quantum ground state. The researchers kept the same antimatter particle trapped for months and manipulated its quantum energy levels using precisely tuned microwaves. With this achievement, physicists can now make more precise comparisons between matter and antimatter. According to CPT symmetry, electrons and positrons should have identical magnetic properties besides their opposite charges. The same research group previously measured the electron's magnetic moment to about one part in 10 trillion, and the new positron system could eventually allow a similar, precise antimatter measurement. Planetary minerals Scientists from Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory and Hopkins published recent findings on MgO, magnesium oxide, and phase transitions. Researchers used powerful lasers to generate shock waves that compressed tiny MgO crystals to pressures as high as 600 gigapascals and temperatures around 13,000 K, reproducing conditions found deep inside planets. Using nanosecond X-ray diffraction and other measurements, they watched the physical crystal structure change. Contrary to the long-standing assumption that the direction of compression should no longer matter at such extreme pressures, they found that MgO underwent dramatically different phase-transition pathways depending on the orientation of the crystal when it was compressed. When MgO was compressed along one crystal direction, it transitioned relatively smoothly from its B1 crystal structure into a denser B2 structure before melting. When compressed along other directions, however, the transition was delayed by roughly 80 GPa, and the material appeared to pass through a temporary disordered state before forming the new structure. Eventually, all orientations completely melted at approximately 572 ± 24 GPa and 13,200 ± 600 K, establishing an exceptionally high experimentally measured melting temperature under planetary-interior conditions.

articles.title: Metalens microscope switches focus with voltage, not moving optics
articles.description: Just as it is difficult for a camera to keep both a nearby flower and a distant mountain sharply focused at the same time, conventional optical microscopes face a similar challenge when imaging structures located at different depths inside the body. Tighter focusing of light improves spatial resolution, but at the same time reduces the depth range over which the image remains sharply focused.

articles.title: Beyond trial and error: Integrating computation, processing, and AI to design high-entropy alloys
articles.description: Designing structural high-entropy alloys (SHEAs) means solving a problem with an enormous number of moving parts: which combinations of composition and processing conditions will yield the phases, microstructures, and mechanical properties a given application demands? Because these alloys mix multiple principal elements in comparable proportions, that question spans length and time scales that no single experiment or model can cover on its own.

articles.title: How antimatter went from Dirac's equation to PET scans and CERN traps
articles.description: These antimatter facts cover 10 discoveries and open questions, from Paul Dirac's 1928 prediction to CERN's antihydrogen experiments and the puzzle of missing antimatter

articles.title: Superman Announces Major New Kryptonian Superpower
articles.description: Superman and the other Kryptonians gain many special abilities when absorbing yellow sunlight, and now yet another power is being introduced.

articles.title: Running Toward a Cure: Reflections at "Next Conversations"
articles.description: "Will AI cure cancer?" As part of the "Next Conversations" series celebrating its 150th anniversary, Hopkins hosted a panel discussion at the Chevy Chase Auditorium on Oct. 14. Moderated by Steve Inskeep, an award-winning journalist and longtime host of NPR's Morning Edition, the discussion brought together Bloomberg Distinguished Professor Ashani Weeraratna, Director of inHealth Precision Medicine Dr. Vasan Yegnasubramanian and Pulitzer Prize-winning author Dr. Siddhartha Mukherjee to reflect on the promise, limitations and ethical complexities of artificial intelligence (AI) in cancer care and research. University President Ronald J. Daniels opened the event by reflecting on the history of cancer care at Hopkins, particularly the vision of Oncology Center Founding Director Albert Owens Jr. to bring scientific discovery and patient care closer together. "How does one take new knowledge and put it to practical human use, and how does one use technology in a human way? How do we keep the patient at the center of our focus when algorithms increasingly shape decisions about their care?" Daniels asked. Building on Daniels' remarks, the panelists turned to the potential applications of AI in cancer care and research. Mukherjee began by proposing a framework for understanding how AI could contribute to advances across different stages of cancer care. "What is AI doing to prevention? What is AI doing to early detection? And what is AI doing to treatment?" Mukherjee posed. Turning to cancer screening, Weeraratna highlighted the Swedish MASAI trial, which investigated the use of AI to assist radiologists in interpreting mammograms. She pointed to the study as an example of how AI could improve the efficiency and accuracy of breast cancer detection. "[The AI screening system] turned out to be more accurate than even having two radiologists reading the mammograms. It reduced the workload by over 40%, but it also reduced error quite significantly of misread mammograms." Beyond traditional imaging methods, Yegnasubramanian discussed AI's potential to analyze complex molecular data, including cell-free DNA found in blood samples. Such technologies could help identify not only the presence of, but also the type of cancer. "We have to know which [cancers] are the ones that are also going to cause harm, so that we don't expose people to treatments that not only do they not need, but may even harm them. The power of our modern computational methods to decipher all of that from the complex measurements we take is really quite extraordinary." Elaborating on the potential of computational methods in cancer treatment, Yegnasubramanian underscored their utility in precision medicine, that is, in selecting individualized treatments and monitoring their effectiveness or signs of recurrence. "This is the promise of precision medicine, finding the right treatment for the right person, and having biomarkers that predict that can be very important." Weeraratna illustrated this approach using personalized mRNA vaccines for melanoma, which are currently being investigated to treat and prevent recurrence of the disease. "You can detect the DNA of each patient in their blood, analyze it through sequencing methodologies, figure out exactly what genes are being expressed, what proteins are being expressed, and then you can target those vaccines to those very specific proteins." With such promising applications on the horizon, then came the inevitable question. Inskeep put it straightforwardly. "Okay, so is AI going to cure cancer? Mukherjee cautioned against such overly-simplistic thinking, noting the inherent complexities within the terms "cure" and "cancer". "There's not one cure and there's not one cancer." Nevertheless, Mukherjee remained optimistic about AI's potential to advance the treatment of certain cancers over the next two decades, particularly through robotic surgery, immunotherapy and vaccines. The prospect of increasingly autonomous medical technologies, however, raised Inskeep's broader question about AI's future in medicine beyond cancer. "Could we envision a computer, with little to no human intervention, diagnosing, arranging the treatment, conducting the surgery, doing almost everything?" In response, Mukherjee distinguished between two forms of AI: "bits to bits," in which algorithms process and generate information, and "bits to atoms," in which AI systems interact with the physical world. He pointed to computationally-driven drug development and robotics as examples of the latter. Mukherjee further considered the implications of AI systems capable of independently improving themselves and interacting with their surroundings. "It should give us pause as we invent these machines, which are neurosymbolic, critically self-improving machines, which interact with the sensory world, and ask the question: What is the difference, then, between human beings and this machine?" Even as AI systems become increasingly sophisticated, their conclusions are not always reliable, for example, due to inaccurate outputs and biases in training data. Beyond diagnosing diseases and determining treatments, however, medicine depends on empathy, trust and the deeply personal relationships between physicians and patients. Weeraratna echoed this sentiment. "You can't underestimate the value of human connection … I would not want to go to a robot doctor. I would want an actual person to tell me what was happening that the robot may or may not have diagnosed," Weeraratna noted. Weeraratna, therefore, emphasized the importance of remaining mindful of the technology's limitations, describing the notion of a partnership, rather than a blind reliance, between physician and AI. Additionally, Mukherjee suggested that AI could strengthen, rather than diminish, the human side of medicine. "I'm not sure I would trust a physician who does not use AI," Mukherjee commented. In elaborating on his statement, Mukherjee referred to AI's ability to rapidly navigate vast amounts of medical literature and automate clinical documentation. Rather than distancing physicians from their patients, such tools could strengthen clinical decision-making while enabling doctors to devote more attention to their patients. Yegnasubramanian similarly envisioned a collaborative relationship in which AI could assist physicians with everything from patient histories to diagnoses and treatment planning, without displacing human judgment. "To me, the fine-tuned sweet spot where I think AI can be very impactful, serve humanity in the best ways, serve medicine in the best ways, is that synergy between the physicians, AI, patients, having both the artificial and human element of this come together and work together," Yegnasubramanian added. However, realizing this vision of collaboration requires more than simply incorporating AI into clinical practice. As medical professionals increasingly rely on computational tools to inform their decisions, their ability to recognize the technology's limitations becomes equally important. Weeraratna cautioned against excessive reliance on AI for the next generation of scientists. "My big concern with AI is not that they use it, but that they allow it to think for them." Weeraratna's concern reflects a broader goal for the relationship between man and machine: instead of taking humans out of medicine, AI may give physicians and researchers better tools to understand diseases, make decisions and care for patients. The question, then, is not simply what AI can do for medicine, but how human minds can responsibly guide it toward new possibilities in patient care. Altogether, while AI may not offer a definitive cure for cancer, it may bring us closer to understanding and treating the disease in ways once thought impossible.

articles.title: Silent bacterial genes yield potential leads for future cancer drugs
articles.description: Natural products produced by microorganisms are a promising source of new drugs. Researchers at the Helmholtz Center for Infection Research (HZI) and its Saarbrücken-based site, the Helmholtz Institute for Pharmaceutical Research Saarland (HIPS), have now discovered a new family of such compounds, elucidated their unusual biosynthesis and developed a way to produce them synthetically.

articles.title: Light-based monitoring could improve quality checks for lab-grown replacement cartilage
articles.description: A new doctoral dissertation by Omar Anwar Elkadi in the field of Applied Physics on near-infrared spectroscopy for the continuous monitoring of tissue-engineered cartilage will be defended at the Faculty of Science, Forestry and Technology, Kuopio campus, of the University of Eastern Finland on Oct. 30.

articles.title: Analog astronauts: How living underwater can prepare humans for space missions
articles.description: The risks and advantages of performing research missions underwater to prepare for space exploration.

articles.title: “Prediction” Markets Were Comically Wrong About the Brazilian Election
articles.description: Flávio Bolsonaro was the overwhelming favorite, right up until the moment he unceremoniously lost. The post “Prediction” Markets Were Comically Wrong About the Brazilian Election appeared first on Futurism.

articles.title: Quantum biology and how it could transform the medical world
articles.description: Two Northwestern professors discuss where the field currently stands and where they hope it can go in just a few decades

articles.title: 5 human emotions that dogs can actually sense — according to animal behaviorists
articles.description: A study of 30 dogs tested whether dogs can sense human emotions by sound, with clear head-turn results for three of six emotions: happiness, fear and sadness

articles.title: Brain stimulation temporarily changes perception of sexualized images of women
articles.description: Applying mild electrical stimulation to the brain temporarily removed a perceptual bias linked to the sexual objectification of women, in the first study of its kind. The study is published in the journal Social Neuroscience.

articles.title: RNA archiving method reveals what a cell did days ago
articles.description: Information on what a cell did a few hours or days ago is generally unavailable to researchers, who can only measure the cell's current status. This is a problem if the aim is to understand how immune responses arise or why individual cancer cells survive treatment.

articles.title: Thousands of students across Oregon celebrate National Farm to School month
articles.description: More than 40,000 students in almost 100 Oregon school districts participated in the "Oregon Crunch at Once" event celebrating Farm to School month.

articles.title: Diamond defects confirm 80-year-old theory of crystal stress
articles.description: For the first time, researchers in Japan have directly mapped several components of the stress field surrounding an atomic-scale flaw in the crystal structure of diamond. Led by Tokuyuki Teraji at Japan's National Institute for Materials Science, the team achieved its result using nitrogen-vacancy (NV) centers in diamond, whose spin states respond differently to stress depending on how they are oriented relative to the stress field.

articles.title: Tiny shifts in iron content tip a potential memory material between competing magnetic states
articles.description: A team of Yale researchers has figured out what gives a magnetic material its mysterious properties, a discovery that could help boost computing memory and the field of "spintronics." Their work is published in Physical Review Letters.

articles.title: Thermal priming enhances heat tolerance and yield in tomatoes after recurrent heat stress
articles.description: High temperatures can significantly impair the growth and yield of crops, including tomatoes. A new study by an international research team led by Dr. Justyna Olas, of the Leibniz Institute for Horticultural Sciences (IGZ), has shown that tomatoes can respond better to subsequent heat stress following moderate heat exposure. The work is published in The Plant Journal.

articles.title: An 'electron waiting room' helps blue titanium dioxide hold light energy longer
articles.description: To produce hydrogen using sunlight, the energy obtained from light must be retained until it can be used in a chemical reaction. However, if an electron that has gained energy from light quickly returns to its original position, it becomes difficult to make use of that energy.

articles.title: Top Economist Finds That AI Has Provided “Zero Financial Payoff” to Companies Outside Tech
articles.description: "There are still no signs of AI boosting productivity growth." The post Top Economist Finds That AI Has Provided “Zero Financial Payoff” to Companies Outside Tech appeared first on Futurism.

articles.title: America's military bases prepare for 90-day doomsday scenario
articles.description: The Pentagon is preparing US military bases for a doomsday scenario in the event a major war breaks out on American soil.
